newsitem.title: USA: R.R. Donnelley hit on non-diverse board.
newsitem.headline: R.R. Donnelley hit on non-diverse board.

text.p: R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co., fighting age and racial discrimination lawsuits, faced further criticism Thursday at its annual shareholders' meeting for not nominating any minorities to its board of directors.

The Rev. Jesse Jackson, speaking from the floor, expressed concern at the lack of diversity on the printing company's board. He called not having a black or Latino director "unacceptable race discrimination."
A Jackson spokeswoman said the civil rights activist bought about $2,000 in Donnelley shares in order to participate in the shareholders' meeting.
In response, acting Chairman John Richman said, "We were very close to getting a minority director, but things fell through."
Jackson also recommended a union representative be named to Donnelley's board as a way of easing an adversarial relationship between labour and management.
"We must replace walls that divide with bridges that unite," said Jackson, a civil rights leader who heads the Rainbow PUSH Action Network.
R.R. Donnelley prints catalogues and newspaper inserts, telephone directories and a score of magazines, including Time, The New Yorker and Sports Illustrated.
Nearly 100 former Donnelley employees marched in protest prior to the meeting, toting placards reading "Equal Protection Under the Law" and "Face the Truth, Settle the Suit."
"Donnelley promised to move expeditiously, but has not made any substantial efforts toward settling the pending lawsuits," Jackson told Reuters before the meeting.
Last December, the company was named in a $500 million class-action suit charging it with racial discrimination based on layoffs, promotions and wages. It has denied the allegations.
The suit claims black and older workers affected by a plant closing, announced in 1993, fared worse than younger white employees in getting reassigned with the company.
"Legal counsel advises us that these suits are without merit," Richman told shareholders, adding that the company would make its formal response to the charges in court.
Richman told Jackson, "Our vision of inclusion is the same as yours. We're making progress."
Donnelley's newly appointed chief executive officer, William Davis, agreed to meet with Jackson and his organisation. "I'm anxious to meet with you," Davis said.

In positioning Donnelley for profitability, Richman said the company would remain focused on strengthening its core U.S. printing business, expanding selectively in worldwide markets and developing a digital-content marketing and distribution infrastructure.

Donnelley posted a 1996 loss of $157.6 million, or $1.04 per share, including a $435 million after-tax restructuring charge and a $48 million after-tax gain on the initial public offerings of Metromail Corp. and Donnelley Enterprises Solutions Inc.
"We know we must improve results in 1997," Richman said, adding, "The core business is mature, but it offers significant opportunities."
